READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO ACTS 13

  1. Chapters 13 and 14 are an account of Paul and Barnabas' first missionary journey. The rest of the book of Acts will be given over to Paul's ministry.

  2. It would be very helpful to turn to the map in the back of your Bible or atlas and follow the geographical locations mentioned in Acts 13 and 14.

  3. There is an obvious transition in Acts 13 and 14 from the leadership of Barnabas to the leadership of Paul.

  4. Notice the series of OT quotes (much like Stephen's sermon)
    1. v. 33 ‒ Ps. 2:7
    2. v. 34 ‒ Isa. 55:3
    3. v. 35 ‒ Ps. 16:10
    4. v. 41 ‒ Hab. 1:5
    5. v. 47 ‒ Isa. 49:6

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Acts 13:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:3 The verse has three AORIST PARTICIPLES describing the spiritual preparations to send out the first missionaries from the church at Antioch.

  1. fasted ( SPECIAL TOPIC: FASTING)
  2. prayed ( SPECIAL TOPIC: EFFECTIVE PRAYER)
  3. laid hands on them ( SPECIAL TOPIC: LAYING ON OF HANDS)

This seems to be the united actions of the whole congregation, not just the other prophets and teachers. The whole church should be involved in Great Commission activities!

▣ "laid their hands on them" This particular verse is one of the ambiguous texts on which our modern practice of ordination is based. However, it is inappropriate as a biblical foundation for our modern denominational practices. There are many physical examples of "laying on of hands" in the Bible.

  1. in the OT for the purpose of
    1. sacrificial identification (cf. Lev. 1:4; 3:2; 4:4; 16:21)
    2. a blessing (cf. Gen. 48:13ff; Matt. 19:13,15)
    3. the commissioning of a successor (cf. Num. 27:23; Deut. 34:9)
  2. In the NT the background is equally as varied
    1. for healing (cf. Luke 4:40; 13:13; Acts 9:17; 28:8)
    2. dedication or commissioning to a task (cf. Acts 6:6; 13:3)
    3. connected with receiving the Holy Spirit or spiritual gifts (cf. Acts 8:17; 19:6; 1 Tim. 4:14; 2 Tim. 1:6)
    4. a reference to the basic teachings of Judaism or the church (cf. Heb. 6:2)

This laying on of hands was not an inaugurating experience. These men were already called, gifted, functioning leaders. It is not a new ministry they are called to, but an expansion of what they were already doing.

Ordination tends to encourage a distinction among believers. It gives credence to the clergy‒laity dichotomy. The Greek word cleros (to inherit by lot) and laos (Greek word for people), when used in the NT, always refers to the entire group of believers. All believers are called, gifted, full time ministers of the gospel (cf. Eph. 4:11-12). There is no biblical evidence for separating believers into hierarchal groups. All believers are gifted for ministry to the Body of Christ (cf. 1 Cor. 12:7, 11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAYING ON OF HANDS

SPECIAL TOPIC: ORDINATION

entries.title: Acts 13:4 "being sent out by the Holy Spirit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:4 "being sent out by the Holy Spirit" This context does not assert the authority of the local church, but the authority of the Spirit. He is that part of the Trinity emphasized in Acts. The "new Messianic age" was known as "the Age of the Spirit." He calls, gifts, directs, convicts, and empowers (cf. John 14:16-17,26; 15:26; 16:7-15). No permanent or effective ministry can occur without His presence and blessing.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY

▣ "Seleucia" This was the port city of Antioch of Syria. It was about fifteen miles southwest. Its name goes back to Alexander the Great's general (Seleucid), who ruled this area after Alexander's death.

▣ "Cyprus" This was Barnabas' home (cf. Acts 4:36) where there was a large Jewish population. In the OT it is known as Kittim. This was not the first Christian witness on this island (cf. Acts 11:19-20).

entries.title: Acts 13:5 "Salamis"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:5 "Salamis" This was the port city on the east coast of the island of Cyprus. It was the commercial center of the island.

▣ "they began to proclaim the word of God in the synagogue" This phrase, "the word of God," refers to the gospel of Jesus Christ. The reason for this is obvious.

  1. these Jews already knew the OT
  2. Jews were the chosen people (cf. Gen. 12:1-3) and had the first opportunity to respond (cf. Acts 3:26; 13:46; 17:2; 18:4,19; 19:8; Rom. 1:16)
  3. in the synagogue services were Gentiles who
    1. had already been attracted to the one true God (i.e., monotheism)
    2. knew the OT ("God-fearers")

This became Paul's regular missionary method wherever there was a synagogue.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

▣ "John" This refers to John Mark in whose home the disciples met (cf. Acts 12:12). He is also the traditional writer of the Gospel of Mark, which seems to record the eyewitness testimony of the Apostle Peter. He is also the cause of the great argument between Paul and Barnabas which split the missionary team (cf. Acts 15:36-41). However, later on Paul mentions John Mark in a positive way (cf. Col. 4:10; 2 Tim. 4:11 and Philemon 24).

SPECIAL TOPIC: JOHN MARK

entries.title: Acts 13:6 "when they had gone through the whole island"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:6 "when they had gone through the whole island" This probably means that they stopped and preached in every synagogue on the island.

▣ "Paphos" This refers to new Paphos, in contradistinction from the older Phoenician city seven miles away. Both of these cities are named after the Phoenician goddess Paphian. This was the god of love also known as Aphrodite, Astarte, Venus, etc. This city was the official political capital of Cyprus.

▣ "Bar-Jesus" This man was a Jewish false prophet. His name means "son of Joshua." We learn from Acts 13:8 that he went by the designation "Elymas the magician." This term "magician" reflects the Greek equivalent of an Aramaic root that means "sorcerer" (cf. Acts 13:10). See note on the Hebrew equivalent in Deut. 18:10 online.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

entries.title: Acts 13:7 "the proconsul, Sergius Paulus"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:7 "the proconsul, Sergius Paulus" There has been much discussion about the historicity of Luke's accounts. Here is a good example of the accuracy of Luke the historian. He calls this man "a proconsul," which meant Cyprus was a Roman Senatorial province. We learn this occurred in A.D. 22 by decree from Augustus. We also learn from a Latin inscription at Soloi that Sergius Paulus began his proconsulship in A.D. 53. The more information archaeology discovers from the Mediterranean world of the first century, the more Luke's historical accuracy is corroborated.

For full note on "proconsul" see Acts 19:35.

▣
NASB  "a man of intelligence"
NKJV, NRSV, TEV  "an intelligent man"
NJB  "who was an extremely intelligent man"
REB  "a learned man"
Peshitta  "a wise man"

This term is used with a wide variety of connotations.

  1. In this context it implies he was able to rule effectively.
  2. Also characterizing him in this way shows that the gospel not only impacted the poor and uneducated, but also the wealthy and educated (cf. Manaen 13:1).
  3. He was interested in magic or spiritual issues (v. 7c).
  4. It is also possible that one of Luke's intents of writing Acts was to show that the gospel did not threaten Roman rule.

entries.title: Acts 13:8 "Elymas"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:8 "Elymas" It seems that this name is a Greek transliteration of

  1. an Arabic term for a wise man (a sage, a diviner, one who can foresee and control the future by manipulating the unseen powers/forces of the unseen realm, AB, vol. 2, p. 487)
  2. an Aramaic word for one who interprets dreams

▣ "magician" This is related to the term "magi," which meant Chaldean-Median wise men, like Daniel (cf. Dan. 2:2; 4:9; Matt. 2:1). However, by Paul's day, it was used of itinerant magicians and wandering quacks in the Greco-Roman world.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

▣ "(for thus his name is translated)" This seems to be an editorial comment by Luke to help his readers understand this term, which was not from a Greek root. Also note another one in v. 9 (NET Bible).

▣ "was opposing them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith" This was a major spiritual confrontation between the light of the gospel and the darkness of superstitious paganism. The radically new message about God and how He interacts with His world, directly challenged the pagan religions of the first century Mediterranean world.

▣ "the faith" This term is used in three specific ways in the NT:

  1. personal trusting in Jesus Christ as a Savior
  2. faithful, godly living (OT sense of faithfulness)
  3. theological content of the gospel (i.e., doctrine, cf. Jude 3, 20, which has the DEFINITE ARTICLE, as it does here)

The same ambiguity is seen in Acts 6:7. Here it seems to refer to #3 because of the ARTICLE and the context. See note at Acts 3:16.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CANON (NT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: FAITH, BELIEVE, or TRUST

entries.title: Acts 13:9 "Paul"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:9 "Paul" Most Jews of Paul's day who lived outside Palestine had two first names, one Jewish, one Roman (cf. Acts 13:9). Paul's Jewish name was "Saul." He, like the ancient King of Israel, was of the tribe of Benjamin (cf. Rom. 11:1; Phil. 3:5). His Roman name in Greek form, "Paul" (Paulos), meant "little." This referred to

  1. his physical stature which was alluded to in a second century non-canonical book, The Acts of Paul, in a chapter about Thessalonica called "Paul and Thekla"
  2. his personal sense of being least of the saints because he originally persecuted the Church (cf. 1 Cor. 15:9; Eph. 3:8; 1 Tim. 1:15)
  3. simply the name given by his parents at birth
  4. "Saul" sounded similar to an effeminate word

Option #3 seems best.

▣ "Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit" The power of the Spirit that guided the early church is described by the term "the filling" (cf. Acts 2:4; 4:8,31; 6:3; 7:55; 9:17; 13:9,52). This ongoing, daily filling of the Spirit is the normal state of all believers (cf. Eph. 5:18). In Acts it is usually associated with a boldness to proclaim the gospel. See full note at Acts 5:17 and SPECIAL TOPIC: FILLED

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT (filling)

▣ "fixed his gaze" See fuller note at Acts 1:10.

entries.title: Acts 13:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:10 Paul characterizes this Jewish false prophet by several phrases.

  1. "full of all deceit," meaning to entrap with a bait (this is the only use of this term in Luke's writings)
  2. "full of all fraud," this is from the Greek word that means to do something lightly or frivolously, but it came to have an evil connotation (cf. Acts 18:14). This term is found only in Acts (cf. Acts 13:10; 18:14).
  3. "son of the devil," this is a Semitic idiom (cf. Acts 3:25; 4:36) for one characterized by the actions of the devil (cf. Matt. 13:38; John 8:38,41,44
    SPECIAL TOPIC: DEVIL)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: SONS OF. . .
  4. "enemy of all righteousness," This term is used several times in Luke's writings involving OT quotes (cf. Luke 1:71,74; 20:43; Acts 2:35). All that is like God, this man was against.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS
  5. Paul uses the inclusive term "all" three times to show this man's complete volitional wickedness

▣ "to make crooked the straight ways of the Lord?" This question expects a "yes" answer. The word "right" or "straight" in the NT reflects the OT concept of righteousness, which meant a standard or measuring reed. The NT terms "crooked" or "perverted" reflect the OT terms for sin, which were a deviation from the standard, which is God Himself. This man made everything crooked (i.e., the opposite of righteousness). He was an enemy of the gospel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "the Lord" This use of kurios refers to YHWH (as does v. 11), who in the OT is regularly called adon.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kuiros)

entries.title: Acts 13:11 "the hand of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:11 "the hand of the Lord" This is a Semitic anthropomorphic phrase referring to the power and presence of YHWH (cf. Luke 1:66; Acts 11:21). In the OT it often refers to God's judgment (cf. Exod. 9:3; 1 Sam. 5:6; Job 19:21; 23:2; Ps. 32:4; 38:2; 39:10), as it does here.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "you will be blind" These powerful descriptive terms of evil and rebellion by which Paul characterizes this man and the form of his temporary divine punishment may reflect Paul's own previous life. He looks back now and sees himself in this Jewish false teacher and his manipulation (cf. Acts 9:8).

Blindness is often used in a parabolic sense of a lack of spiritual receptivity (cf. John 9; Acts 9; also note Deut. 28:28-29).

▣ "a mist" This is a known medical term (i.e., Galen).

entries.title: Acts 13:12 "believed when he saw what happened"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:12 "believed when he saw what happened" This is the same Greek word (pisteuō, the NOUN can be translated as "believe," "faith," or "trust") used throughout the NT for genuine belief. This governor responded to the gospel message. One man's eyes were closed (literally); one man's eyes were opened (metaphorically). This is the mystery of belief and unbelief (cf. John 9). See additional note at Acts 16:14.

It is this theological issue that develops into the sovereignty vs. freewill debate. Why do some humans who hear the gospel respond positively and some negatively? There have been many theories through the centuries of church history.

  1. the fall of mankind blinds some to the truth of the gospel (human responsibility, Isa. 6:9-10)
  2. Satan prevents some from understanding the gospel (cf. 2 Cor. 4:4; Matt. 13:4,19)
  3. God enables "some" to understand and respond (Augustine, Calvin, i.e., John 6:37,44,65)

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD HARDENED

SPECIAL TOPIC: FAITH, BELIEVE, or TRUST

entries.title: Acts 13:13 "Paul and his companions"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:13 "Paul and his companions" Obviously the leadership has changed. From now on in the book of Acts Paul's name will be listed first.

▣ "Perga in Pamphylia" Perga was the largest city of the small Roman coastal province of Pamphylia (mid-southern Turkey). It was located several miles inland to discourage attacks by sea-faring raiders.

Apparently Paul did not preach here at this time, but did so later (cf. Acts 14:25). There is no historical evidence of a Christian group in this area for several hundred years. He merely passed through this coastal region.

▣ "John left them and returned to Jerusalem" Luke records this event, but gives no clue as to why (nor does any other NT author).

SPECIAL TOPIC: JOHN MARK

entries.title: Acts 13:14 "Pisidian Antioch"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:14 "Pisidian Antioch" This literally means "Antioch towards Pisidia" because it was located in the ethnic area of Phrygia the Roman Province of Galatia. This was a distinct ethnic group, probably from Europe.

▣ "on the Sabbath day" This would denote from sundown on Friday to sundown on Saturday. The Jews counted time from evening to evening, following Genesis 1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SABBATH

▣ "sat down" This may be an idiom denoting someone who was to speak in the synagogue. Rabbis always taught while seated (cf. Matt. 5:1; Luke 4:20). The synagogues regularly allowed itinerant visitors to speak if they wished (cf. Acts 13:15).

entries.title: Acts 13:15 "the reading of the Law and the Prophets"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:15 "the reading of the Law and the Prophets" This was the part of the typical order of service in a synagogue in Jesus' day. Originally only the Law of Moses was read, but Antiochus IV Epiphanes forbade this in 163 B.C. The Jews then substituted the reading of the Prophets. During the Maccabeen revolt, Judaism was restored and both the Law and the Prophets were continued to be read together as a basic format of weekly synagogue services (cf. Acts 13:27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYNAGOGUE SERVICE

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW CANON

▣ "the synagogue officials" These were the men in charge of building maintenance and the order of worship (cf. Luke 8:41,49). They often invited guests to speak.

▣ "if you have any word of exhortation" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE, assumed to be true from the perspective of the author of for his literary purposes. This was a normal aspect of synagogue worship. Paul took full advantage of the opportunity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK GRAMMATICAL TERMS, VII

entries.title: Acts 13:16 "Paul stood up"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:16 "Paul stood up" Usually Jewish teachers sit when they teach; however, it was the Greco-Roman custom to stand while teaching. Paul modified his manner and presentation to the audience.

▣ "motioning with his hand" Paul gestured for quiet. Luke mentions this eyewitness detail often (cf. Acts 12:17; 13:16; 19:33; 21:40).

entries.title: Acts 13:16b "Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:16b "Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen" There were two groups present, Jews and Gentile "God-fearers" (cf. Acts 13:26; 10:2,22,35). This sermon is very similar to Stephen's sermon of Acts 7. In many ways Paul was deeply influenced by Stephen's understanding of the OT and the gospel. See Contextual Insights to Acts 7.

For "fear" see SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

entries.title: Acts 13:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:17 Paul began his review of OT history with the call of the Patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in Genesis) and the captivity and deliverance from Egypt (Exodus-Deuteronomy).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "with an uplifted arm He led them out" This is typical OT imagery (cf. LXX Exod. 6;1,6; also note Ps. 136:10-22) of YHWH's power and presence in physical terms. It is similar to the anthropomorphic phrase, "His right arm." The Bible must speak of God in human vocabulary (i.e., anthropomorphism) even though He is an eternal, non-physical, all pervasive Spirit. These biblical analogies are the source of many misunderstandings and literal overstatements. The Bible must speak of God in analogy, metaphor, and negation. God is far greater than fallen, time-bound, earth-bound humans can comprehend or express!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD

entries.title: Acts 13:18 "For a period of about forty years He put up with them in the wilderness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:18 "For a period of about forty years He put up with them in the wilderness" This reflects Deut. 1:31 and could be translated "fed as a nurse" (cf. MSS A, C). This reflects the OT books of Exodus and Numbers.

The term "forty" is often a round number. Literally the time from Horeb to Shittim was thirty-eight years with a two year period at Horeb (Sinai).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #7

entries.title: Acts 13:19 "destroyed seven nations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:19 "destroyed seven nations" The nations of Palestine can be characterized in several ways.

  1. collective terms
    1. Canaanite (i.e., lowlander, cf. Gen. 10:18-29; Jdgs. 1:1)
    2. Amorite (i.e., highlander, cf. Gen. 15:16)
  2. two nations (Canaanites, Perizzites, cf. Gen. 13:7; 34:30; Jdgs. 1:4-5)
  3. three nations (Hivites, Canaanites, Hittites, cf. Exod. 23:28)
  4. six nations (Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite, Jebusite, cf. Exod. 3:8,17; 33:2; 34:11; Deut. 20:17; Josh. 9:1; 12:8)
  5. seven nations (Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites, cf. Deut. 7:1; Josh. 3:10; 24:11)
  6. ten nations (Kenite, Kenizzite, Kadmonite, Hittite, Perizzite, Rephaim, Amorite, Canaanite, Girgashite, Jebusite, cf. Gen. 15:19-21)

SPECIAL TOPIC: PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE

▣ "an inheritance" The triple compound term kata + klēros + nemō is common in the Septuagint, but is used only here in the NT (other texts have kata + klēros + didōmi). It implies the casting of lots as a means of dividing the Promised Land among the tribes (cf. Josh. 13-19).

The word klēros is where we get the English word "clergy," but in the NT it always refers to the body of believers, not an elite group!

▣ "four hundred and fifty years" This number seems to be arrived at by:

  1. 400 year bondage in Egypt (cf. Gen. 15:13)
  2. 40 year wilderness wandering period (cf. Exod. 16:35; Num. 14:33-34; 32:13)
  3. 7-10 year conquest (cf. Josh. 14:7,10)

The Textus Receptus (KJV) moves the number to Acts 13:20 and seems to include the period of the Judges (following Josephus, Antiq. 8.3.1), but this wording is not in the older and better uncial Greek manuscripts (cf. א, A, B, C), which fits better with 1 Kgs. 6:1 dating. The dash found in the NASB is to accentuate the proper place of the number.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE EXODUS (uncertainties)

entries.title: Acts 13:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 13:20 This refers to the period from the book of Judges through 1 Samuel 7.

entries.title: Acts 13:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:21 This refers to 1 Samuel 8-10.

▣ "for forty years" This time phrase is not found in the OT unless the OT manuscript problem connected to 1 Sam. 13:1 includes "forty" (NIV). Josephus, Antiq. 6.14.9 also mentions that Saul reigned "forty" years. The Septuagint just omits the entire sentence and starts with 1 Sam. 3:2. "Forty" was obviously a rabbinical tradition.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #7

entries.title: Acts 13:22 "I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after My heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:22 "I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after My heart" This is not a direct quote from the OT but it seems to be a combination of Psalm 89:20 and 1 Samuel 13:14. It needs to be remembered that this sermon by Paul follows the basic pattern of Stephen's historical rendition in Acts 7. That David can be called a man after God's heart, when he was such a notorious sinner (cf. Ps. 32,51; 2 Samuel 11), is a great encouragement to all believers.

This combination quote implies several things.

  1. This was a standard practice with the rabbis, which explains many of the unusual OT quotes in the NT (see SPECIAL TOPIC: RABBINICAL HERMENEUTICAL TECHNIQUES
  2. This was already a part of Christian catechism. Paul often quotes from early Christian hymns and possibly other literature (i.e., Phil. 2:6-11; Col. 1:15-16; 1 Tim. 3:16; 2 Tim. 2:11-13).
  3. This quote is unique to Paul and shows that Luke must have gotten his summary of this first recorded message of Paul in Acts from Paul himself.
NASB, NKJV  "who will do all My will"
NRSV  "who will carry out all my wishes"
TEV  "who will do all I want him to do"
NJB  "who will perform my entire will"
REB  "he will carry out all my purposes"
Peshitta  "to do my will"

This verse is a combination of OT allusions. This part of the sentence is not in the OT passages. In the OT context Saul was disobedient and rejected. But David's life also had disobedience. God works with imperfect humans to accomplish His redemptive plan. See "Introduction to Acts," "Purpose and Structure," #10.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Acts 13:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:23 This verse points back to all the OT promises.

  1. a redemption through the seed of a woman, Gen, 3:15
  2. a ruler from Judah, Gen. 49:10
  3. a coming leader like Moses, the Prophet, Deut. 18:15,18
  4. a leader from David, 2 Sam. 7; Ps. 132:11; Isa. 11:1,10; Matt. 1:1
  5. a suffering servant, Isa. 52:13-53:12 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: A SUFFERING MESSIAH)
  6. a savior, Luke 2:11; Matt. 1:21; John 1:29; 4:42; Acts 5:31 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: OUR SAVIOR)

For Luke #4 is prominent (cf. Luke 1:32,69; 2:4; 3:31; Acts 2:29-31; 13:22-23). The Messiah would be of Jesse's line (cf. Isa. 9:7; 11:1,10; 16:5). Notice how Paul jumps from David to Jesus. The NT tends to focus on

  1. the Abrahamic covenant
  2. the Davidic covenant

which is a Messianic focus.

entries.title: Acts 13:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:24 John the Baptist's ministry and message is described in Mark 1:1-8; Matt. 3:1-11; Luke 3:2-17; John 1:6-8,19-28. John fulfilled the prophecies of Mal. 3:1; 4:5-6. He was the last OT prophet. His preaching of repentance also set the pattern for Jesus' early preaching (cf. Matt. 4:17; Mark 1:14-15).

John spoke of a Coming One, greater than himself (cf. Matt. 3:11; Mark 1:7; Luke 3:16; John 1:27,30; Acts 13:25).

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS' BAPTISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: OT TITLES FOR THE SPECIAL COMING ONE

entries.title: Acts 13:25 "while John was completing his course"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:25 "while John was completing his course" God had a specific task for John to perform. John's public ministry only lasted eighteen months. But, what a year and a half it was, filled with the Spirit's power and preparing the way for the Messiah.

Because of the power and success of John's ministry, many hoped that he was the promised Coming One. There had been no prophetic voice in Israel for 400 years! John makes it very plain in several gospel texts that he is not the Messiah, but His forerunner (cf. Matt. 3:11; Mark 1:7; Luke 3:15-17; John 1:20,27).

entries.title: Acts 13:26 "sons of Abraham's family, and those among you who fear God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:26 "sons of Abraham's family, and those among you who fear God" This refers to both the Jewish hearers (or proselytes) and the Gentiles (God-fearers) attached to Judaism's monotheism and morality.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

▣ "this salvation" This is referring to God's promise to redeem fallen humanity through a Messiah (cf. Gen. 3:15). It includes Gentiles (cf. Gen. 12:5; Exod. 19:5-6; and Acts 28:28 and 13:46).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Acts 13:27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 13:27 This is such a tragic verse. It succinctly summarizes the blindness of the Jews in Jerusalem about the Scriptures even though they read them continuously. By missing the prophetic signs (cf. Genesis 3:15; Psalm 22; Isaiah 53; Zechariah 9-14) and prophecies (Isaiah, Jonah) they became the prophetic sign! He came to His own, but His own received Him not (cf. John 1:11-12).

entries.title: Acts 13:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 13:28 Acts records again and again the spiritual responsibility of the Jews in Jerusalem (cf. Acts 2:23,36; 3:13-15; 4:10; 5:30; 7:52; 10:;39; 13:27-28). Jesus was innocent of every charge and should have been released (cf. Luke 23:4,14,22).

entries.title: Acts 13:29 "they. . .they"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:29 "they. . .they" These must refer to different groups.

  1. The first were those who sought Jesus' death (i.e., Jewish leadership, the crowd before Pilate).
  2. The second involves those who wanted a proper burial.
  3. This could have involved
    1. sincere Jewish people who saw the injustice (similar to Acts 8:2, involving the burial of Stephen)
    2. secret disciples like Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus (cf. John 19:38-42)

▣ "all that was written concerning Him" Jesus' life was one of fulfilled prophecy. One strong evidence for the inspiration of the Bible and the Messiahship of Jesus of Nazareth is predictive prophecy (cf. Luke 22:22; 24:32; Acts 2:23; 3:18; 4:28; 10:43; 13:29; 24:14; 26:22).
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)

It is surely true that many of the details of Jesus' life, which we in the church today call prophecy, are in a sense typology. Many events happened in the life of Israel which later seem to also occur in Jesus' life (one example, Hosea 11:1). Often ambiguous, oblique passages, which would not have been understood in context as prophetic, seem to jump to life as one views Jesus' earthly experience (ex. Psalm 22; Isaiah 53). It takes inspiration and a sense of the flow of redemptive history to fully appreciate the OT foreshadowing of Jesus. I would also add that although inspired NT writers use typology, even allegory, that modern teachers and preachers should not use this method of interpretation! See Richard N. Longnecker, Biblical Exegesis in the Apostolic Period and my Biblical Interpretation Seminar online at www.freebiblecommentary.org

SPECIAL TOPIC: TYPOLOGY

▣ "the cross" See notes at Acts 5:30 and 10:39.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CRUCIFIXION

entries.title: Acts 13:30,33,34,37 "But God raised Him from the dead"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:30,33,34,37 "But God raised Him from the dead" The NT affirms that all three persons of the Trinity were active in Jesus' resurrection:

  1. the Spirit (cf. Rom. 8:11)
  2. the Son (cf. John 2:19-22; 10:17-18)
  3. the Father (cf. Acts 2:24,32; 3:15,26; 4:10; 5:30; 10:40; 13:30,33,34,37; 17:31; Rom. 6:4,9; 10:9; 1 Cor. 6:14; 2 Cor. 4:14; Gal. 1:1; Eph. 1:20; Col. 2:12; 1 Thess. 1:10).

This was the Father's confirmation of the truth of Jesus' life and teachings. This is a major aspect of the Kerygma (i.e., content of the sermons in Acts).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE EARLY CHURCH

SPECIAL TOPIC: RESURRECTION

entries.title: Acts 13:31 "for many days"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:31 "for many days" Acts 1:3 says "forty days." However, forty is a common OT round number.

▣ "He appeared" See SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS' POST RESURRECTION APPEARANCES

▣ "the very ones who are now His witnesses to the people" The resurrected Jesus told the group of His disciples assembled in Acts 1 (i.e., His ascension) that they were to be "His witnesses" throughout the world (i.e., Matt. 28:19-20; Luke 24:46-47; Acts 1:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ASCENSION

entries.title: Acts 13:32 "the promise made to the fathers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:32 "the promise made to the fathers" This refers to the initial promise of YHWH to Abraham for a land and a seed (cf. Gen. 12:1-3). This same promise of God's presence and blessing was repeated to the Patriarchs and to their children (cf. Isa. 44:3; 54:13; Joel 2:32). The OT focuses on the land, while the NT focuses on "the seed." Paul alludes to this very promise in Rom. 1:2-3 and also note Romans 4.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Acts 13:33
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:33 This quote from Ps. 2:7, which is a royal Messianic psalm about the conflict and victory of God's Promised Messiah (see detailed exegetical notes online). Jesus had been killed by evil forces (human and demonic), but God had raised Him to victory (cf. Rom. 1:4).

This verse and Rom. 1:4 were used by early heretics (adoptionists) to assert that Jesus became Messiah at the resurrection. There is surely a NT emphasis on Jesus being affirmed and glorified because of His obedience, but this must not be taken in isolation from His preexistent glory and Deity (cf. John 1:1-5,9-18; Phil. 2:6-11; Col. 1:13-18; Heb. 1:2-3).

The VERB "raised" (anistēmi) is used in several senses.

  1. in Matt. 22:24 and implied in Acts 13:23, it refers to raising up a descendant
  2. in Acts 3:22 it is used of God raising up "a prophet like Moses," referring to Deut. 18:15 (cf. Acts 7:37)
  3. in Acts 3:25-26 it is used of God raising up "His Servant" (lit. "Child"), referring to the Abrahamic promises in Gen. 12:3; 22:18
  4. in Acts 13:22 it is used of God raising up a Davidic King, the Messiah
  5. in Acts 2:32; 13:30,34,37; 17:31 it is used of God raising Jesus from the dead
  6. in John 6:39,40 it refers to the resurrection of believers
  7. in reality God raised Jesus to Messianic leadership at His baptism by John (see F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, pp. 171-172)

SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: RESURRECTION

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS' BAPTISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: ADOPTIONISM (early heresy)

entries.title: Acts 13:34 "no longer to return to decay"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:34 "no longer to return to decay" This statement from Psalm 16 refers to Jesus' death and resurrection. He was the first to be resurrected (first fruits of the dead, cf. 1 Cor. 15:20) rather than resuscitated. Many people were brought back to physical life in the Bible, but they all had to die again (i.e., Lazarus). Enoch and Elijah were "translated" to heaven without death, but they were not resurrected.

▣ "I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David" This is a quote from Isa. 55:3 from the LXX. The quote includes the PLURAL "sure blessings," but does not specify to what this refers. It is something that passed from God to David, to Jesus, then to His followers (PLURAL "you" in the quote). The OT context shows the significance of "you" (cf. Isa. 55:4-5 LXX, "Behold, I have made him a testimony among the Gentiles, a prince and commander to the Gentiles. Nations which know thee not, shall call upon thee, and peoples which are not acquainted with thee, shall flee to thee for refuge, for the sake of the Lord thy God, the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified thee," The Septuagint, Zondervan, 1976, p. 890).

The blessings and promises to David (i.e., Jews) are now the blessing and promises of the Gentiles (i.e., the entire human race). See full note at Romans 9-11.

entries.title: Acts 13:35-37
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:35-37 This is the same argument used earlier in Peter's Pentecost sermon (cf. Acts 2:24-32), also taken from Psalm 16. These early sermons in Acts reflect an early Christian catechism. Several OT Messianic texts were strung together. Therefore, often the PRONOUNS and details do not seem to be relevant to the central purpose of the NT author, which was to affirm the physical resurrection of Jesus and the decay of David.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE EARLY CHURCH

entries.title: Acts 13:36 "fell asleep"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 13:36 "fell asleep" Sleep is an OT euphemism for death. This imagery has been taken literally to promote a view of the spiritual state of believers between death and the Second Coming (i.e., 1 Thess. 4:13-18). For a good brief discussion of the different views on this theological issue, see Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, 2nd, pp. 1179-1190.

entries.title: Acts 13:38
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:38 Paul is using an OT augmented argument, as does Peter (Acts 2) and Stephen (Acts 7) to reach these synagogue hearers. This is also true of the Gospel of Matthew.
SPECIAL TOPIC: Rabbinical Hermeneutics

Paul promises a full and complete forgiveness of sins, which Judaism could not provide (cf. Acts 13:39), to all who trust Jesus as the Christ (i.e., "This One," Acts 13:38,39).

The promise of forgiveness in Jesus is repeated several times by Luke.

  1. Luke 24:47 ‒ to all
  2. Acts 5:31 ‒ to Israel
  3. Acts 10:43 ‒ to all
  4. Acts 13:38,39 ‒ to Israel and God fearing Gentiles
  5. Acts 26:18 ‒ to Israel

entries.title: Acts 13:39 "and through Him everyone"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:39 "and through Him everyone" Notice the universal element. God loves all humans made in His image and all humans have the opportunity to respond to Him by faith (cf. Acts 10:43; Isa. 42:1,4,6,10-12; 55; Ezek. 18:23,32; Joel 2:28,32; Luke 24:47; John 3:16; 4:42; Rom. 3:22,29,30; 10:9-13; 1 Tim. 2:4; 4:10; Titus 2:11; 2 Peter 3:9; 1 John 2:1; 4:14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "who believes" This is the covenantal requirement for all! Forgiveness is a gift of God through Christ to all, but it must be received by faith (i.e., Eph. 2:8-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FAITH. BELIEVE, or TRUST

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

NASB, NKJV  "is freed from all things" (Acts 13:39)
NRSV  "is set free from all those sins" (Acts 13:39)
TEV  "is set free from all the sins" (Acts 13:39)
NJB  "justification from all sins" (Acts 13:38)
REB  "is acquitted of everything"
Peshitta  "are justified from all things"

This is literally "justified" (PRESENT PASSIVE INDICATIVE). This is a legal term which describes our standing before God by means of Jesus Christ's imputed righteousness (cf. Romans 4; 2 Cor. 5:21). In Hebrew "righteousness," "justify," originally referred metaphorically to a "river reed." It reflects an OT construction term used as imagery for God as the standard or ruler by which judgement is made.

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "which you could not be freed through the Law of Moses" This was Paul's major theological point (cf. Rom. 3:19-30). The Mosaic law was a tutor to bring us to an understanding of our personal sin and to cause us to desire Christ (cf. Gal. 3:23-29; the book of Hebrews). The OT Law is not a means of salvation, because all sinned (cf. Rom. 3:9-18,23; Gal. 3:22). It had become a death sentence, a curse (cf. Col. 2:14). Jesus bore "the curse" of the OT performance-based law that no one could keep because of the fall of mankind recorded in Genesis 3 (cf. Gal. 3:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S VIEWS OF THE MOSAIC LAW

entries.title: Acts 13:40-41
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:40-41 Paul calls on his hearers (PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE) to respond by trusting Jesus as the Promised Messiah, as the only way to receive forgiveness (cf. John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Tim. 2:5; 1 John 5:10-12).

He quotes Hab. 1:5 from the Septuagint as a warning. In other places in Paul's writings he quotes Hab. 2:4 as an appropriate faith response (cf. Rom. 1:17; Gal. 3:11). Paul preaches for a decision. Intellectual assent is not enough; a complete personal surrender to Jesus as the only hope is required. This initial faith and repentant response must be matched by daily Christlike living (cf. Matthew 7; 13).

Verse 41 describes the shocking new methodology of salvation of the New Covenant in Christ (see full note online at Jer. 31:31-34).

entries.title: Acts 13:42
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:42 This shows the power of the Spirit

  1. using Paul's sermon
  2. the hunger (i.e., "kept begging. . .") for forgiveness and restoration with God within the hearts of humans made in God's image (i.e., Gen. 1:26-27)
13:43
NASB, Peshitta  "God-fearing proselytes"
NKJV  "devout proselytes"
NRSV  "devout converts to Judaism"
TEV  "Gentiles who had been converted to Judaism"
NJB  "devout converts"
REB  "Gentile worshipers"

This phrase is literally "worshiping proselytes." This is a different group from the "ones fearing God" of Acts 13:16,26 (cf. Acts 10:2,22,35).

Verse 43 refers to those Gentiles who had officially become Jews (i.e., "God fearing proselytes"). This required

  1. self baptism in the presence of witnesses
  2. circumcision for males
  3. offering a sacrifice at the temple in Jerusalem when possible

There are a few references to Jewish proselytes in the NT (cf. Matt. 23;15; Acts 2:11; 6:5; 13:43).

▣ "urging them to continue in the grace of God" From the context it is difficult to define this phrase.

  1. some of these hearers may have already responded to the gospel in their hearts
  2. those who were faithful to what they understood of the grace of God in the OT are urged to continue to seek God and listen to Paul again (cf. Acts 13:44)
  3. true salvation is an initial choice followed by daily (hourly) choices (cf. Acts 11:23)

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSEVERANCE

entries.title: Acts 13:44
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:44 Paul's message had an obvious impact. This is also hyperbole. Not everyone in the city attended. See G. B. Caird, The Langauge and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 22, 110-117, 121.

NASB, NRSV, TEV  "the word of the Lord"
NKJV, NJB, REB, Peshitta  "the word of God"

There is a Greek manuscript variant at this point.

  1. "Lord" is in MSS P74, א, A, B2
  2. "God" is in MSS B, C, E

The UBS4 puts "Lord" in the text, but rates it "C" (difficulty deciding). As with so many variants, this does not change the sense of the text. The gospel is a divine revelation about Jesus, the Messiah/Christ, by God the Father through the Holy Spirit.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TEXTUAL CRITICISM

entries.title: Acts 13:45 "when the Jews saw the crowd. . .jealousy"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:45 "when the Jews saw the crowd. . .jealousy" Whether it was the large turnout or the large number of Gentiles in the crowd that caused the jealousy is uncertain in this context. Jealousy is attributed to Jewish leadership both in Jerusalem and the Diaspora. (cf. Matt. 27:18; Mark 15:10; Acts 17:5).

Later in the book of Romans Paul develops the theological problem of Jewish unbelief (cf. Romans 9-11). He asserts that God has temporarily blinded Israel so that the Gentiles might be saved. However, God will use the salvation of the Gentiles as a means (i.e., jealousy) to cause Israel to respond to Christ, so that all believers will be united through the gospel (cf. Eph. 2:11-3:13).

The problem is when does Israel turn to Christ? The same question could be asked of Zech. 12:10. Is this prophecy related to the early church, which was made up of believing Jews, or to a future period? Jealousy is meant for a redemptive purpose (cf. Rom. 10:19; 11:11,14), but the jealousy in this text causes unbelief!

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO OT COVENANT PROMISES SEEM SO DIFFERENT FROM NT COVENANT PROMISES?

▣ "they were fill with jealousy" See full note at Acts 3:10. For "filling" see note at Acts 5:17 and SPECIAL TOPIC: FILLED

▣ "were blaspheming" As these Jews defended their traditions and attacked Paul's preaching, they themselves were guilty of blasphemy. There is no middle ground here. Either Judaism or Christianity is a true reflection of God's will. They both are exclusive!

entries.title: Acts 13:46 "spoke out boldly"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:46 "spoke out boldly" This is one of the signs in Acts of being Spirit-filled.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BOLDNESS

▣ "'It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first'" This was the pattern of early missionary preaching (cf. Rom. 1:16). The Jews had priority, but God had included Gentiles (cf. Romans 9-11). Those in the synagogue knew their OT and could check the prophecies. Acts has a series of texts on this ministry pattern (cf. Acts 3:26; 9:20; 13:5,14; 16:13; 17:2,10,17).

▣ "'you repudiate it'" This is a strong VERB (PRESENT MIDDLE INDICATIVE) used several times in the Septuagint. Its basic meaning is "to thrust away." It was used of the Israelites in Stephen's sermon (cf. Acts 7:39). It is also used by Paul in Rom. 11:1-2 to assert that God has not rejected His people, but they have rejected His Son, His only means of salvation (cf. John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Tim. 2:5; John 5:10-12), His full revelation.

▣ "and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life'" Wow, what a condemnation. It is not God who rejected them but they rejected God and His Son! Consequences are based on the necessary corrollary of human freewill. How can humans be judged for that in which they have no choice?!

This is a devastating phrase. One who

  1. repudiates the gospel
  2. judges himelf
  3. is unworthy of eternal life

I am becoming more and more convinced of the biblical basis on "limited immortality." Only those who believe and walk in the truth of the gospel have eternal life.

Several YouTube videos have opened my eyes to this issue.

  1. Edward Fudge, "The Fire That Consumes"  YouTube One Hour Lecture
  2. Steve Gregg, "Hell — Three Christian Views"  YouTube Lecture - 1:34:57

It is difficult to hold the concept of predestination, which is emphasized so often in Acts, with the concept of mandated individual personal response. No one can come to faith without the drawing of the Spirit (cf. John 6:44,65), but we are judged by whether we respond or not. By their rejection of Paul and Barnabas' preaching of the gospel, they revealed their true selves (cf. John 3:17-21). The blame for lack of response cannot be placed on God. He has provided a way, His Son, but He is the only way! This is the mystery of "unbelief"!

For me, this theological tension is best explained as the reality of

  1. God's unconditional covenant to redeem mankind made in His image
  2. the conditional covenant of the divine mandate of a human response (both initially and unto death)

The best theological category to hold together this biblical tension is the concept of "covenant."

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELECTION

▣ "we are turning to the Gentiles" This becomes a regular pattern of gospel proclamation (cf. Acts 18:6; 22:21; 26:20; 28:28; Rom. 1:16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTICVE PLAN

entries.title: Acts 13:47
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:47 This is a quote from Isa. 49:6 (cf. Isa. 42:6) from the Septuagint. Simeon used this quote as a blessing on Jesus in Luke 2:32 to affirm His Messianic task of universal redemption. It is even possible that the "light" in the context refers to Paul and Barnabas' preaching of the gospel to these Gentiles (cf. "Use of the Old Testament in the New," by Darrell Boch, p. 97 in Foundations for Biblical Interpretation, Broadman & Holman Publishers, 1994). Now Paul uses it to show the universal proclamation of the universal gospel! See full list of texts at Acts 13:39.

The ending phrase, "to the end of the earth," may be an allusion to Acts 1:8. It highlights the universality of the gospel. Oh, how I love "whosoever," "as many as," "everyone who." The door to forgiveness, peace, and full fellowship with God is open in Christ! Come (i.e., Isaiah 5; Rev. 22:17)!

entries.title: Acts 13:48 "When the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:48 "When the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord" Many of these had been in the synagogue for years and had never heard the inclusive, universal message of God's love and acceptance of all humanity by faith in Messiah. When they heard it they enthusiastically received it (cf. Acts 28:28) and passed it on to others (cf. Acts 13:49).

▣ "as many as had been appointed to eternal life believed" This is a clear statement of predestination (so common in the rabbis' and Intertestamental Jewish literature), but it is in the same ambiguous relationship as all NT passages that relate to the paradox of God's choice (i.e., John 6:37,44,65; 17:2,6,9) and human's free will (cf. John 1:12; 3:16; Phil. 2:12,13; Heb. 5:9). The VERB is a PLUPERFECT PASSIVE PERIPHRASTIC that comes from a military term (tassō) which means to "enroll" or "appoint." See note at v. 46.

This concept of enrolling refers to "the two books" that God keeps (cf. Dan. 7:10; Rev. 20:12).

  1. First is the Book of the Deeds of men (cf. Ps. 56:8; 139:16; Isa. 65:6; and Mal. 3:16).
  2. The other is the Book of Life (cf. Exod. 32:32; Ps. 69:28; Isa. 4:3; Dan. 12:1; Luke 10:20; Phil. 4:3; Heb. 12:23; Rev. 3:5; 13:8; 17:8; 20:12-15; 21:27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO BOOKS OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELECTION/PREDESTINATION AND THE NEED FOR A THEOLOGICAL BALANCE

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE

entries.title: Acts 13:50 "But the Jews incited the devout women of prominence"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:50 "But the Jews incited the devout women of prominence" This text gives historical and cultural setting of the exalted place of women in Asia Minor in the first century (cf. Acts 16:14; 17:4).

In this context it refers to proselytes to Judaism who were also leaders in the community or were married to the civic leaders. A. T. Robertson, Word Pictures in the New Testament, vol. 3, p. 201, makes the point that Gentile women were greatly attracted to Judaism (cf. Strabo 7:2 and Juvenal 6:542) because of its morality.

▣ "instigated a persecution against Paul" Paul refers to this in 2 Tim. 3:11.

entries.title: Acts 13:51 "they shook off the dust of their feet"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:51 "they shook off the dust of their feet" This is a Jewish sign of rejection (cf. Matt. 10:14; Mark 6:11; Luke 9:5; 10:11). It is uncertain whether this refers to

  1. dust on their feet and sandals from walking
  2. dust on their robes which was kicked up when they were working

▣ "Iconium" This was a major city of Lycaonia, located in the Roman province of Galatia. It was about eighty miles east, southeast of Pisidian Antioch and directly north of Lystra.

entries.title: Acts 13:52 "continually filled with joy"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:52 "continually filled with joy" This is an IMPERFECT PASSIVE INDICATIVE which can mean the beginning of an action or the repeat of an action in past time. The NASB, 1995 update, takes it in the second sense. Only the Holy Spirit can give joy amidst persecution (cf. Rom. 5:3; James 1:2ff; 1 Peter 4:12ff).

The phrase "the disciples" is ambiguous. Does it refer to the new believers, the missionary team, or both? See SPECIAL TOPIC: DISCIPLES

For "filled" see full note at Acts 5:12 and SPECIAL TOPIC: FILLED

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why can 13:2-3 not be used as a proof-text for ordination by a select group?
  2. Why did Paul preach in the synagogue first?
  3. Why did John Mark leave the mission team? (cf. Acts 13:13)
  4. How is Acts 13:39 related to Galatians 3?
  5. Explain Acts 13:48b in relation to predestination and human free will.

entries.title: Acts 14:1 "Iconium"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:1 "Iconium" There is a second century non-canonical book known as The Acts of Paul and Thekla, which is reported to be Paul's activities in Iconium. This book possibly contains the only physical descriptions of Paul ever recorded: short, bald, bow legged, heavy eyebrows, and protruding eyes (cf. 2 Cor. 10:10). It is quite uninspired and yet reflects the impact that the Apostle Paul had in this region of Asia Minor. Most of this area was in the Roman Province of Galatia.

▣ "entered the synagogue" This was Paul and Barnabas' regular pattern (cf. Acts 9:20; 13:5,14; 14:1; 18:4,19; Rom. 1:16). These hearers, both Jews and God-fearing Greeks, would be familiar with the OT prophecies and promises.

▣ "a large number of people believed, both of Jews and of Greeks" This phrase shows the purpose of Acts. The gospel is spreading vigorously among various people groups. The implications of the OT promises to all humanity (cf. Gen. 1:26-27; 3:15; 12:3) are now being realized.
SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

"Believe" is a major theological concept in Scripture. Remember, most NT authors (except Luke) were Hebrew thinkers writing in Koine Greek. So, modern interpreters must seek the intended meaning in the Koine Greek translation of the OT called the Septuagint, and not simply Greek lexicons.

These summary statements relating to the rapid growth of the church are characteristic of Luke's writings. See "Introduction to Acts," "Purpose and Structure," #1,3.

entries.content:
